title: Letters to the Emperors & Kings
subtitle: Universal Calling: Messages to Heraclius, Chosroes, Negus, and Muqawqis
summary: The crafting of the silver signet ring, the global diplomatic vision of Islam, Heraclius's dramatic interrogation of Abu Sufyan in Jerusalem, Chosroes tearing the letter in rage and the prophecy of his ruin, and the reverent responses of the Negus and Muqawqis.

sections.text: The Universal Calling & The Silver Seal

With the southern border pacified by the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ initiated the global proclamation of Islam. The divine mission was never intended solely for the Arabs; it was a universal message revealed for all humanity. In late 6 AH and early 7 AH, the Prophet summoned his companions to announce diplomatic missions to the superpowers and regional monarchs of the ancient world.

When companions informed him that imperial courts refused to accept any document that did not bear an official seal, the Prophet commanded the crafting of a silver signet ring. Upon its bezel were carved three words arranged vertically: 'Muhammad' at the bottom, 'Rasul' in the middle, and 'Allah' at the top, ensuring that the Divine Name reigned supreme above all.

Six seasoned companions rode out simultaneously across the deserts: Dihyah ibn Khalifah al-Kalbi carried the letter to Heraclius, Emperor of the Byzantine Roman Empire; Abdullah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi was sent to Chosroes Parvez, King of the Persian Sasanian Empire; Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri carried the missive to the Negus (Al-Najashi) of Abyssinia; Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah journeyed to Al-Muqawqis, governor of Egypt and Alexandria; Shuja' ibn Wahb was dispatched to Al-Harith ibn Abi Shamir al-Ghassani, client king of Syria; and Salit ibn Amr rode to Hawdhah ibn Ali in Al-Yamamah.
Heraclius & The Interrogation of Abu Sufyan

When Dihyah delivered the letter to Heraclius in Jerusalem (Aelia), the emperor summoned Arabian merchants visiting Gaza to interrogate them regarding Muhammad's background. Abu Sufyan, still an idolater, was brought forward as the Prophet's closest kinsman. In a masterclass of imperial inquiry recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, Heraclius asked eleven searching questions: 'Does his family possess noble lineage?' Abu Sufyan admitted: 'Yes.' 'Has anyone among his ancestors been a king?' 'No.' 'Do the noble people follow him or the poor?' 'Rather the poor and weak.' 'Do any apostatize out of displeasure with his religion after embracing it?' 'No.' 'Does he break his promises?' 'No.'

Heraclius sighed and delivered an astonishing historical verdict: 'If what you say is true, he is indeed a prophet, and he will soon conquer the very ground beneath these two feet of mine! Were I with him, I would wash his feet.' Yet political fear of losing his imperial throne prevented Heraclius from embracing the faith.

In stark contrast, when Abdullah ibn Hudhafah delivered the prophetic letter to Chosroes in Ctesiphon (Al-Mada'in), the Persian emperor erupted in tyrannical fury upon seeing the Prophet's name written before his own. He seized the parchment and tore it to shreds, screaming: 'A lowly subject dares to write his name before mine!' When this was reported to the Prophet ﷺ, he made a solemn supplication: 'May Allah tear his empire to pieces!' Within a short time, Chosroes was overthrown and murdered by his own son Sheroe, and within two decades, the entire Sasanian Empire dissolved into history.
The Reverence of the Negus & Muqawqis

In Abyssinia, the Negus received the letter with profound reverence, placing it over his eyes, descending from his royal throne to sit upon the earth, and renewing his heartfelt submission to Islam. In Alexandria, Al-Muqawqis treated Hatib with regal courtesy, admitting that a final prophet was expected, though he had thought he would arise in Syria. He sent generous diplomatic gifts, including two honorable Coptic noblewomen—Maria and Shirin—and the white mule Duldul. Through these historic embassies, the voice of Islam crossed imperial borders, establishing its universal mission to all humanity.

references.notes: Ibn Abbas, from Abu Sufyan: Heraclius questioned him at Jerusalem during the truce. The old addition of Bukhari 2936–2941 was not re-opened and is not cited.

references.title: Sahih Muslim
references.author: Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj (d. 261 AH)
references.notes: Anas: the Prophet wrote to Kisra, to Caesar, to the Negus, and to every tyrant, calling them to Allah. This Negus was not the one for whom he had prayed the funeral prayer. Hadiths 1773 and 1775 were not re-opened, so they are not cited. The wording of the letters in the sirah is not copied here as if it were this Hadith.
